archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, pass-starved)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff under Jeff Hafley has a team that wants to win on the ground and on early downs, but it has no working passing game and no pass rush, and so far it cannot win at all.

report.headline: A real run game stuck inside a team that can't pass or rush the passer
report.take:
Miami is 0-5 and the record isn't hiding anything. The Dolphins rank last in net EPA and last in point differential per game, 29th in offensive EPA and 29th in defensive EPA allowed. This continues a slide the history shows clearly: a top-five offense in 2023, a 7-10 team ranked 27th in net EPA last year, and now a new coach starting over with Malik Willis taking every snap. The wins-over-expected figure of -1.15 says they've been a little unlucky, but the differential only implies about one win. This is a bad team with a few bad bounces, not a decent one.

The offense has picked an identity and the numbers back the choice. Miami's pass rate over expected is 31st in the league, and the run game is better than its 20th-ranked rushing EPA looks. The line ranks 2nd in yards before contact, and the last two weeks produced the two best rushing games of the year: +4.9 rushing EPA at Minnesota and 217 rushing yards against Cincinnati. The problem is what happens when Willis drops back. Pressure allowed ranks 31st, he holds the ball longer than any quarterback in the league, the sack rate is 27th, and the passing EPA in those same two games was -12.4 and -11.4. Those two weeks were the closest losses of the season, and they came from running well enough to hide a passing game that fell apart.

The defense splits in a similar way. Against the run it is respectable: 14th in rushing EPA allowed, with a missed-tackle rate that ranks 7th. It has also kept No. 1 receivers in check, 2nd-best in PPR points allowed to WR1s relative to their averages. But it has 4 sacks all season, last in the league, and without pressure everything underneath leaks. Pass EPA allowed is 31st, short-pass EPA allowed is 30th, third-down conversion rate allowed is 31st, and tight ends are feasting at 0.90 EPA a target, worst in the league. Add special teams at 31st and a -4 turnover differential, and the field-position bill is too large for a 14-point offense to pay.

The outlook is grim, with a couple of soft spots. Eleven games remain, and the Bills appear twice and the Lions once, against top-three offenses. LAC at 0-6, Indianapolis and two meetings with the Jets are the realistic chances to win. A bye week gave Hafley time to fix how the ball gets out, and that is the variable that matters most. If Willis keeps taking sacks and turning the ball over, the run game alone won't be enough against decent defenses.

strengths.title: Line creates space in the run game
strengths.body: Miami's backs average 3.45 yards before contact, 2nd in the league, so the blocking up front is real even though a 29th-ranked stuff rate shows the misses are costly. Once the staff leaned into it, the run game turned positive. Rushing EPA was +4.9 at Minnesota and +9.0 with 217 yards against Cincinnati. It should hold up because it's built on blocking, not breakaway luck, though Jonah Savaiinaea's ankle bears watching.

strengths.title: Sound run defense and tackling
strengths.body: The front holds up on the ground: 14th in rushing EPA allowed, with a missed-tackle rate that ranks 7th. Miami doesn't give away free yards after the catch or the handoff. That lets this defense keep games close against run-first or limited offenses, even though it can't win on passing downs.

strengths.title: Top receivers held in check
strengths.body: Opposing WR1s have scored well under their usual output against Miami, 2nd-best in the league by that measure. Opponents have answered by throwing to tight ends and backs, so this reflects how the coverage is shaded more than a lockdown secondary. It still matters against offenses that run through a single receiver.

concerns.title: Passing game collapses under pressure
concerns.body: Willis faces pressure on 28% of dropbacks (31st) while holding the ball longer than any quarterback in the league, which produces sacks and drive-killing negative plays. The passing EPA in Weeks 4 and 5 was the worst of the season even as the run game took off. The line and the quarterback's processing are both part of this, and nothing in five games suggests it fixes itself without a scheme change.

concerns.title: No pass rush, no third-down stops
concerns.body: Miami has 4 sacks, last in the league, with the lowest sack rate. Opposing quarterbacks get clean pockets, and it shows: pass EPA allowed ranks 31st, short-pass EPA 30th, and third-down conversions allowed 31st. Tight ends draw a far larger share of targets than usual and lead the league in EPA a target against this defense. This is a talent problem, not bad luck.

concerns.title: Hidden yards bleed the other way
concerns.body: Special teams cost Miami about three and a half points a game, 31st in the league, and the offense has 8 turnovers against 4 takeaways. For an offense scoring 14 a game, giving up field position and possessions is how close games turn into two-score losses. Turnover margins swing a lot, but the special-teams hole has been consistent.

trend.note: Margins narrowed in Weeks 4 and 5 once Miami committed to the run, including a cover at Minnesota and a push against Cincinnati. But the passing numbers got worse at the same time, so the team found a different way to lose rather than getting better.

nextGame.headline: Run-first Miami runs into a stout Jets front off the bye
nextGame.body:
Miami comes off a bye into a division road game as a 4.5-point underdog, with the Book's total at 38.5, a low-scoring script. The matchup cuts against Miami's new identity. The Jets rank 4th in rushing EPA allowed and 6th in sack rate, which is the worst pairing for an offense that wants to run and can't protect when it has to throw. Miami's best hope is the Jets offense, 19th in EPA and 27th in scoring, which is weak on the ground (23rd in rushing EPA) and gives up sacks at the 30th-ranked rate, though Miami has the league's weakest pass rush to take advantage.

The Jets are without RB Breece Hall, G Dylan Parham, WR Adonai Mitchell and DE Joseph Ossai, all ruled out. That thins a run game that was already weak and takes away a pass rusher. Miami's list is longer and more uncertain: G Jonah Savaiinaea (ankle) and WR Caleb Douglas (ankle) were limited and are questionable, starting S Michael Taaffe (chest) and CB JuJu Brents (stinger) are questionable, and CB Storm Duck is listed out. A secondary missing two or three regulars is a serious problem for a defense that already ranks 31st against the pass.

waysToWin.title: Win an ugly, low-scoring game
waysToWin.body: With Hall out, the Jets run game, already 23rd in EPA, has little to work with, and Miami's run defense is solid. If Miami forces Geno Smith into long third downs, the 38.5 total plays into the underdog's hands. A game in the teens favors a team with Miami's ball-control approach.

waysToWin.title: Quick passing to beat the rush
waysToWin.body: The Jets are only 22nd against short passes, and the bye gave Miami time to shorten Willis's reads. Getting the ball out before the Jets' pass rush arrives with Malik Washington and the backs could neutralize the matchup's biggest mismatch. Doing it would turn the Jets' front into a non-factor.

waysToWin.title: Cash in on Jets penalties
waysToWin.body: The Jets commit 8.7 penalties a game, 28th in the league. Free first downs are how an offense with a 37.7% success rate keeps drives going. Miami needs a couple of those gifts to finish drives with points.

waysToLose.title: Jets pass rush overwhelms protection
waysToLose.body: The Jets rank 6th in sack rate. Miami allows pressure at the 31st-ranked rate, and Willis holds the ball longer than anyone. Passing downs could become sacks and turnovers, as they did in the 3-turnover loss to Cincinnati.

waysToLose.title: Run game stalls against a top front
waysToLose.body: Miami's recent improvement came from the ground game, and the Jets are 4th in rushing EPA allowed. If early downs go nowhere, Miami has to throw, and its passing EPA ranks 27th. That leaves the offense without a plan B.

waysToLose.title: Smith extends drives on third down
waysToLose.body: Miami allows third-down conversions at the 31st-ranked rate and has the fewest sacks in the league. A depleted secondary makes it worse. Smith gets clean pockets and time to find tight ends and backs underneath, and long drives in a low-total game are probably enough for New York.

nextGame.watch: How fast Willis gets rid of the ball on early downs: if the bye produced a quicker passing game, Miami can stay in it; if not, the Jets' rush decides the game.

restOfSeason.body:
The record will move off zero, but not much. Five games of bottom-five rankings on both sides of the ball are hard to explain away, and the slightly negative wins over expected suggests one extra loss at most, not a hidden good team. The run blocking and run defense are sustainable. The passing offense and pass defense are structural problems that a bye won't fix, and special teams have been a steady drain. The schedule includes two games against Buffalo's top-ranked offense, plus Detroit, New England twice, Denver, Chicago and Green Bay.

The realistic wins sit in the softer stretch: Indianapolis on the road, the Jets at home, and an LAC team that is 0-6 with the league's worst offense. Some turnover luck should even out and add a point or two to the scoring, but this offense lacks the passing game to reach league-average scoring. Expect a bottom-three finish and an offseason built around quarterback and pass rush.
swingFactors: Whether a post-bye quick-game plan cuts Willis's sacks and turnovers
Health of a secondary missing Taaffe, Brents and Duck
Finding any pass rush to stop third downs

confidence.note: Only five games, but every major ranking points the same way and matches last year's decline.
